archetype.name: Pocket Passer (precision timing)
archetype.definition: A seventh-year distributor who wins from the shotgun with anticipation and ball placement rather than his legs or raw tight-window aggression, and who has ranked at or near the top of the league in completion over expected for most of his career.

report.headline: Downfield precision is real; a 7.8% touchdown rate is what cools first.
report.take:
Burrow has always been an accuracy quarterback. He led the league in CPOE in 2021 (6.64) and ranked third in 2024 (6.787). This season he has pushed past both: a 9.46 CPOE ranks second, he completes 74% of his throws, and he leads the position with 2.88 touchdowns and 298.3 yards a game. Cincinnati leans on that. The Bengals pass 9 points more often than situation predicts, the most in the league, behind a run game that ranks 17th in EPA. This is a full-volume, quarterback-driven offense, and its passing EPA ranks second in the league.

The value comes almost entirely from throws past 10 air yards. His 93 attempts of 10-plus yards have added 98.3 EPA, while his 203 throws under 10 have added just 7, and throws behind the line have cost 14.9. The intermediate window is where he has been startling: 0.951 EPA per attempt with a 20.1 CPOE on 67 throws. Tee Higgins (0.825 EPA per target) has been the main beneficiary. He is doing this while throwing into fewer tight windows: aggressiveness is down 4.2 points from last year to 13.18. He is hitting open windows on schedule rather than forcing throws. Behind a line that allows hits at the sixth-highest rate in the league (27th of 32), his pressure-to-sack rate of 18.6% ranks seventh. With a 2.66-second time to throw, the ball comes out before the rush gets home.

What the line hides is how hot some of it is running. A 7.8% touchdown rate against a league average of 4.3 is the clearest example. So are 16 red-zone touchdowns on 44 attempts with a 19.1 CPOE inside the 20, and a 20-point CPOE on intermediate throws. None of these are rates a quarterback holds over a full season, even this one. The ball security also isn't as clean as the efficiency suggests. His bad-throw rate is up 5.1 points on last year's league-best 5%. His six interceptions rank 35th of 49. Three of those came in the Tennessee shootout, which lifted his last-three interception rate to 2.8%. The 10.1% bad-throw rate is close to his 2021 level and still ranks sixth, so this is a reversion to his normal rather than a decline, but the turnovers are real.

The arc is upward. Weeks 1 and 2 both produced negative passing EPA. The last three games, all wins, averaged 0.456 EPA per dropback, 341.7 yards and four touchdowns. That stretch is his ceiling, not his new baseline. The core holds, though: elite accuracy, top-of-league volume, and an offense that will keep throwing. Expect touchdown totals to come down from a 49-touchdown pace while the yardage and efficiency stay among the best at the position.

strengths.title: Accuracy well beyond expectation
strengths.body: His 9.46 CPOE ranks second, and the gains are concentrated where throws are hardest: 20.1 CPOE on intermediate attempts. This is a career trait, with a league-leading CPOE in 2021 and third in 2024. The skill will last even if this season's peak level eases back toward the 6-7 range of his best years.

strengths.title: Value lives past ten yards
strengths.body: Throws of 10-plus air yards have added 98.3 EPA, and his 26 deep shots average 1.328 EPA. Two outside receivers who both produce (Higgins 0.825 and Chase 0.561 EPA per target) mean coverage can't roll to one side. The per-play rates will cool, but the structure that produces them should hold.

strengths.title: Beats a leaky line with timing
strengths.body: Cincinnati allows hits at a bottom-six rate, yet only 18.6% of his pressures become sacks, seventh-best, and his 4.8% sack rate is 2.5 points under the league average. In past seasons he turned a far larger share of pressures into sacks, so this improvement is newer and deserves a little caution. The quick, on-schedule release it rests on looks repeatable.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate is running hot
concerns.body: A 7.8% touchdown rate, third at the position, and 16 red-zone scores on 44 attempts are the most regression-prone parts of his line. Even his 43-touchdown 2024 didn't need a pace like this one's 49. Expect fewer scores per game while the yardage holds.

concerns.title: Interceptions creeping back
concerns.body: Six interceptions rank 35th of 49, the last three games ran a 2.8% interception rate, and his bad-throw rate is up 5.1 points from last season. That is closer to his 2021-24 norm than a real flaw. But he has always paid for his downfield volume with turnovers, and that cost is returning.

concerns.title: Underneath game adds little
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have cost 14.9 EPA, and Chase Brown's 45 targets average -0.291 EPA. That is mostly scheme (screens and outlets), and it doesn't hurt him while the deep game hits. But it leaves the offense with little to fall back on when downfield windows close. When the Bengals lead by nine-plus, his EPA drops to -0.103, a game-script pullback rather than a skill issue.

trend.note: Negative passing EPA in both of the first two games gave way to 13.9-plus EPA in five of the last six. The last three averaged 0.456 EPA per dropback, against a season mark of 0.271.

nextGame.headline: Stingy Steelers defense, but soft exactly where Burrow does damage
nextGame.body:
Pittsburgh's defense is good overall: sixth in EPA, seventh against the pass, fourth in sack rate. It allows only 12.1 PPR points and 0.88 touchdowns a game to quarterbacks, both among the league's lowest. The weakness is downfield, where it ranks 23rd in deep EPA allowed and 22nd in explosive pass rate. That is the part of the field where Burrow's season lives. Underneath, Pittsburgh ranks eighth, so dink-and-dunk won't work, but that was never his engine. He already put 14.7 EPA on this defense in Week 3, losing a 30-27 shootout. Pittsburgh's run defense (sixth) pushes offenses to pass, and the Bengals throw more than anyone anyway, so volume should be there. The Steelers' own offense runs well (first in rush EPA) and passes poorly (26th), which points to a slower, possession-heavy script and fewer total drives.

On availability, Cincinnati is without tight end Erick All Jr. (ACL, 32% of snaps) for the year, which thins the tight end room behind Mike Gesicki. Andrei Iosivas could come off IR this week, adding a third receiver. Burrow's own report is a stale Week 2 questionable tag with full practice, and the site lists him active. For Pittsburgh, the two corners ruled out, Echols and Slaughter, have played 6% and 0% of snaps, so the starting secondary is intact. Michael Pittman Jr.'s absence mainly limits Pittsburgh's ability to keep pace through the air.

keyMatchups.title: Intermediate and deep game vs soft safeties
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh's deep defense ranks 23rd and allows explosive passes at a bottom-third rate. Burrow's 10-plus air-yard throws have produced nearly all of his EPA. If the Steelers can't fix this from Week 3, his efficiency should hold even against a top-ten unit.

keyMatchups.title: Shadowing Chase, leaking elsewhere
keyMatchups.body: Opposing lead receivers have managed just -0.02 EPA per target against Pittsburgh, third-stingiest, while second receivers (0.22) and top tight ends (0.45, 30th) find room. That points the ball toward Higgins and Gesicki, who already have his two best per-target marks.

keyMatchups.title: Pass rush vs a leaky line
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh's sack rate ranks fourth, and Cincinnati's line gives up hits at a bottom-six rate. Burrow's quick release has kept pressures from becoming sacks. Whether that holds here decides whether he has time to get the ball downfield.

nextGame.watch: Whether Higgins and Gesicki keep winning between the hashes at 10-20 yards while Pittsburgh's coverage leans toward Chase.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume and accuracy are durable. This offense passes more than any in the league, and Burrow's completion-over-expected edge has been a feature of his career, not a hot month. Expect him to stay near the top of the position in yards and efficiency, roughly 270-320 passing yards a game. What regresses is scoring. The red-zone CPOE and the 7.8% touchdown rate should settle, putting him nearer two to three touchdowns a game than the four of his last three. Efficiency should land around 0.17-0.28 EPA per dropback rather than the 0.456 of that stretch.

The risks sit up front and in the turnover column. A line that allows hits at a bottom-six rate has been covered by his release timing. Against the better pass rushes left, that cover could slip and push him into the underneath game, which has done little all year. Interceptions should stay in the 0.6-1.0 per game range, the price of how much he throws past the sticks.
swingFactors: Pass protection holding up against top pass rushes
How far the red-zone touchdown rate regresses
Receiver depth: Iosivas's return and tight end snaps after All's injury

confidence.note: Eight games consistent with his career profile, but several key splits are hot on small samples.
